The lighthouse at the northern point of the bay was built in eighteen sixty-three, after a run of wrecks that had alarmed the merchants of the town enough to raise a subscription for a light. The first keeper, a taciturn man named Alder, kept a daily journal in which he recorded the weather, the passing ships and the state of the oil lamps. His entries are short and largely without comment, though now and then a line betrays irritation at a visiting inspector or quiet satisfaction at a calm sea.

For thirty years the light burned whale oil, then colza, then paraffin, and the keepers changed with the fuels. The station passed from one family to another, and children were born in the small stone cottage behind the tower and later buried in the churchyard above the village. Supplies came by boat when the weather allowed and by cart along the cliff path when it did not, and the keepers learned to plan for weeks of isolation without complaint.

The winter of eighteen ninety-four is remembered in the station records for a gale that carried away part of the outer wall and left the tower standing in a cloud of spray for three days. The keeper at the time wrote that the lantern glass held, that the lamp was trimmed twice a night as usual, and that he had not slept. A later hand has added a note in the margin, in pencil, that the man's wife had died that autumn and that he had refused leave.

By the nineteen twenties the light had been electrified and the staff reduced to two men and a dog. The dog, according to the log, was named Brindle and was afraid of the foghorn. The keepers' work grew easier and lonelier at once: easier because the lamps no longer needed constant trimming, lonelier because there were fewer people to share the watch, and because the visiting inspectors came less often and stayed for shorter periods.

The automation of the station in nineteen eighty-one was described in the local paper as the end of an era, and the last keeper, a young man who had served only four years, was photographed on the gallery with his hands in his pockets, looking not at the camera but at the sea. He told the reporter that he would miss the sound of the wind in the lantern room and that he did not expect to sleep well on land. His wife, who had never lived at the station, said that he talked about it for the rest of his life.

Since then the tower has been maintained by a trust, opened to visitors in summer and repainted twice. The light still turns at night, though it is now a sealed electric unit that no one has to tend. On clear evenings, from the headland, the beam can be seen sweeping the water in a slow and entirely regular rhythm, and visitors often remark that it looks the same as it must have looked a hundred years ago, which is true in the way that a shell held to the ear is true of the sea: the shape is the same and the substance has gone entirely.
